lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: From living tissue to a readable section
lessons.subtitle: The routine paraffin sequence, artifacts, and what each microscope adds

visual.caption: Routine processing replaces water with a hard medium so a thin, stainable slice can be made.

items.label: 1. Fix
items.detail: Formalin cross-links proteins, stops autolysis, and preserves relationships.

items.label: 2. Dehydrate
items.detail: Increasing alcohol removes water because paraffin is not water-miscible.

items.label: 3. Clear
items.detail: An organic solvent such as xylene replaces alcohol and mixes with paraffin.

items.label: 4. Infiltrate and embed
items.detail: Molten paraffin enters tissue and hardens as a supporting block.

items.label: 5. Section and stain
items.detail: A microtome cuts thin sections; paraffin is removed before aqueous staining.

essentials: Dehydration immediately precedes clearing; clearing immediately precedes paraffin infiltration.
The objective lens largely determines light-microscope resolution and useful magnification.
TEM shows internal ultrastructure in thin sections; SEM shows three-dimensional surface topography.
Frozen sections are rapid and preserve lipids or enzyme activity better, but morphology is usually less crisp.
Shrinkage, folds, tears, precipitate, and extraction of lipid are processing artifacts, not real structures.

traps.wrong: Clearing removes tissue water directly.
traps.right: Alcohol first removes water; clearing solvent then replaces the alcohol.

traps.wrong: More magnification always reveals more detail.
traps.right: Resolution, not enlargement alone, determines whether two close points can be distinguished.

recognition: TEM images are flat grayscale views of internal membranes and organelles.
SEM images have a shadowed, three-dimensional surface appearance.
Empty round spaces in routine adipose sections usually represent dissolved lipid.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 1; TUMS INTRODUCTION teacher deck, slides 7-22.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Stain targets at a glance
lessons.subtitle: Match the molecule, tissue component, and expected color

visual.caption: Choose a stain from the chemical target, then use color as confirmation.

items.label: H&E
items.detail: Hematoxylin colors acidic, nucleic-acid-rich structures blue-purple; eosin colors basic proteins, cytoplasm, and collagen pink.

items.label: PAS
items.detail: Carbohydrate-rich structures such as glycogen, basement membrane, and mucins become magenta.

items.label: Elastic fibers
items.detail: Orcein gives dark-brown elastic fibers; the teacher table assigns blue-black fibers to Weigert elastic stain.

items.label: Silver
items.detail: Argyrophilic reticular fibers, nerve fibers, and fungi are rendered brown-black or black.

items.label: Trichromes
items.detail: Masson: collagen blue-green and muscle red. Mallory: deep-blue collagen/bone, red muscle, orange keratin. AZAN strongly separates blue ECM from red muscle.

items.label: Blood and granules
items.detail: Wright differentiates blood cells; toluidine blue shows mast-cell granule metachromasia.

essentials: Basophilia reflects anionic macromolecules, especially DNA, ribosomal RNA, and rough ER.
Eosinophilia reflects proteins rich in positively charged groups, including cytoplasmic proteins and collagen.
Immunohistochemistry uses labeled antibodies to localize a specific antigen rather than a broad chemical class.
Enzyme histochemistry preserves and demonstrates catalytic activity; autoradiography tracks radiolabeled molecules.
A stain's target is more reliable than color alone because protocols can vary.

traps.wrong: PAS is a general protein stain.
traps.right: PAS detects carbohydrate-rich material and makes it magenta.

traps.wrong: Orcein and silver stain identify the same fibers.
traps.right: Orcein highlights elastic fibers; silver methods classically reveal reticular fibers.

recognition: A magenta basement membrane or brush border suggests PAS.
A delicate branching black mesh around cells suggests silver-stained reticular fibers.
Blue-green collagen beside red muscle suggests Masson's trichrome.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 1; TUMS INTRODUCTION teacher stain table, slides 14-16.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: The membrane decides what crosses and how cells hear
lessons.subtitle: Fluid mosaic structure, transport routes, endocytosis, and receptor logic

visual.caption: Membrane proteins convert selective movement or an external signal into a cellular response.

items.label: Bilayer
items.detail: Amphipathic phospholipids form an asymmetric fluid barrier; cholesterol buffers fluidity and permeability.

items.label: Passive routes
items.detail: Simple diffusion crosses lipid; channels and carriers mediate facilitated diffusion down an electrochemical gradient.

items.label: Active routes
items.detail: Pumps use ATP directly; coupled transport uses a preexisting ion gradient.

items.label: Vesicular routes
items.detail: Phagocytosis takes large particles; pinocytosis takes fluid; receptor-mediated endocytosis concentrates selected cargo in clathrin-coated pits.

items.label: Transcytosis
items.detail: Endocytosis at one cell surface, vesicular transport across the cell, then exocytosis at the opposite surface.

items.label: Signal range
items.detail: Endocrine travels in blood; paracrine acts nearby; autocrine acts on the secreting cell; juxtacrine requires contact.

essentials: The glycocalyx is on the extracellular surface and supports protection, adhesion, and recognition.
Integral proteins span or embed in the bilayer; peripheral proteins attach more loosely to a surface.
Lipid rafts concentrate cholesterol, sphingolipids, receptors, and signaling proteins.
Hydrophilic ligands generally use surface receptors; steroid and thyroid hormones bind intracellular receptors.
A receptor can amplify a small extracellular signal through second messengers and kinase cascades.

traps.wrong: Facilitated diffusion uses ATP because it uses a carrier.
traps.right: It uses a protein but still moves down the gradient without direct energy.

traps.wrong: Transcytosis ends in a lysosome.
traps.right: Transcytosis delivers intact cargo to the opposite cell surface.

recognition: A bristle-like external coat on EM is glycocalyx.
A coated invagination with a polygonal cytoplasmic coat suggests clathrin-mediated uptake.
Multiple small flask-shaped membrane pits suggest caveolae.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 2; TUMS lecture 1 deck, membrane, transport, and signaling sections.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Protein and membrane traffic through the cell
lessons.subtitle: Use organelle morphology to predict what a cell makes and where cargo goes

visual.caption: Secreted and membrane proteins follow a vectorial RER-to-Golgi pathway.

items.label: Free ribosome
items.detail: Makes proteins that remain in cytosol or enter nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisomes.

items.label: RER
items.detail: A signal peptide directs the ribosome to RER for synthesis of secreted, lysosomal, and membrane proteins.

items.label: Cis Golgi
items.detail: Receives transport vesicles from RER and begins further modification.

items.label: Trans Golgi
items.detail: Sorts and packages cargo for secretion, membrane insertion, or endosomal-lysosomal delivery.

items.label: Lysosome
items.detail: Acid hydrolases digest material from endocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy.

essentials: RER is basophilic because its ribosomes contain abundant rRNA; protein-secreting cells show prominent RER and Golgi.
SER supports lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification, glycogen metabolism, and calcium storage in muscle.
Mitochondria have a double membrane and cristae; their abundance tracks ATP demand.
Peroxisomes oxidize very-long-chain fatty acids and use catalase to handle hydrogen peroxide.
Proteasomes degrade ubiquitin-tagged cytosolic proteins; lysosomes digest membrane-bound cargo and organelles.

traps.wrong: All proteins are synthesized on RER-bound ribosomes.
traps.right: Translation begins on free ribosomes; only proteins with the proper signal are directed to RER.

traps.wrong: The cis Golgi is the shipping face.
traps.right: Cis receives from ER; trans sorts and ships toward final destinations.

recognition: Parallel flattened cisternae studded with dots identify RER.
Smooth anastomosing tubules without ribosomes identify SER.
Stacked curved cisternae with many nearby vesicles identify Golgi.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 2; TUMS lecture 1 organelle and trafficking sections.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Three cytoskeletal systems, three jobs
lessons.subtitle: Diameter, motor, function, and the difference between an organelle and an inclusion

visual.caption: Size rises from actin to intermediate filaments to microtubules; functions shift from force to tensile strength to tracks.

items.label: Actin microfilaments
items.detail: About 7 nm; cell cortex, microvilli, contraction with myosin, migration, and cytokinesis.

items.label: Intermediate filaments
items.detail: About 10 nm; stable tensile support. Keratin marks epithelia, vimentin mesenchyme, desmin muscle, GFAP astrocytes.

items.label: Microtubules
items.detail: About 25 nm; tubulin tracks for kinesin and dynein, mitotic spindle, cilia, and centrioles.

items.label: Motile cilium
items.detail: A 9+2 axoneme bends through dynein; its basal body has nine triplet microtubules.

items.label: Inclusions
items.detail: Nonliving, usually temporary cytoplasmic deposits such as lipid droplets, glycogen, melanin, or lipofuscin.

essentials: Kinesin usually walks toward the microtubule plus end; dynein usually walks toward the minus end.
Primary cilia are usually nonmotile 9+0 sensory structures; motile cilia typically have 9+2 organization.
Centrioles and basal bodies contain nine peripheral triplets without a central pair.
Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown residual-body pigment that accumulates with age in long-lived cells.
Intermediate-filament markers help identify a cell's tissue of origin.

traps.wrong: Microvilli contain microtubules like cilia.
traps.right: Microvilli have actin cores; cilia have microtubular axonemes.

traps.wrong: A lipid droplet is a membrane-bound organelle.
traps.right: It is a cytoplasmic inclusion with a phospholipid monolayer, not a classic bilayer organelle.

recognition: A ciliary cross-section with nine doublets around two central microtubules is motile 9+2.
A cartwheel-like ring of nine triplets is a centriole or basal body.
Fine brown perinuclear granules in an old long-lived cell suggest lipofuscin.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 2; TUMS lecture 1 cytoskeleton and inclusion sections.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.topic: Nucleus, cell cycle, and cell death
lessons.title: Read the nucleus to read the cell
lessons.subtitle: Chromatin state, nuclear transport, checkpoints, mitosis, apoptosis, and necrosis

visual.caption: A cell passes checkpoints before DNA replication and chromosome separation; damage can divert it to apoptosis.

items.label: G1
items.detail: Growth and preparation; the restriction checkpoint asks whether size, nutrients, signals, and DNA are suitable.

items.label: S
items.detail: DNA is replicated and centrosomes duplicate; chromosome number is unchanged although DNA content doubles.

items.label: G2
items.detail: The cell checks replicated DNA and prepares the mitotic apparatus.

items.label: Mitosis
items.detail: Condense, align, separate sister chromatids, rebuild nuclei, then divide cytoplasm by an actin-myosin ring.

items.label: Apoptosis
items.detail: Caspase-driven cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and apoptotic bodies occur with little inflammation.

items.label: Necrosis
items.detail: Cell swelling and membrane rupture release contents and provoke inflammation.

essentials: Euchromatin is pale, dispersed, and transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is dark and condensed.
The nucleolus makes rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits, so it is prominent in protein-producing cells.
Nuclear pores mediate selective two-way traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm.
The spindle checkpoint prevents anaphase until all kinetochores are properly attached.
Apoptosis preserves membrane integrity until fragments are phagocytosed; necrosis disrupts the membrane.

traps.wrong: DNA replication doubles chromosome number in S phase.
traps.right: It doubles DNA content; chromosome number is counted by centromeres and stays the same until chromatids separate.

traps.wrong: Apoptotic cells swell and cause intense inflammation.
traps.right: They shrink and fragment into membrane-bound bodies with minimal inflammation.

recognition: A pale nucleus with a large nucleolus signals active transcription and ribosome production.
Dense peripheral chromatin and small membrane-bound fragments suggest apoptosis.
Chromosomes aligned at the equator identify metaphase.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 3; TUMS lecture 1 chromatin, cell-cycle, and death sections.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Classify an epithelium in two decisions
lessons.subtitle: Count layers at the basement membrane, then name the shape at the free surface

visual.caption: Layer number predicts barrier strength; apical cell shape predicts the final name.

items.label: Simple squamous
items.detail: One thin layer for exchange or lubrication: endothelium, mesothelium, alveoli.

items.label: Simple cuboidal
items.detail: Round central nuclei in cells as tall as wide: small ducts, kidney tubules, thyroid follicles.

items.label: Simple columnar
items.detail: Tall cells with basal oval nuclei: gut and gallbladder; may bear microvilli or cilia.

items.label: Pseudostratified columnar
items.detail: Every cell contacts basement membrane, but nuclei lie at different heights; often ciliated with goblet cells.

items.label: Stratified squamous
items.detail: Many layers resist abrasion; surface cells are flat. Keratinized epidermis is dry; nonkeratinized mucosa is moist.

items.label: Urothelium
items.detail: Variable thickness with large dome-shaped umbrella cells; stretches in urinary passages.

essentials: All epithelial cells are closely packed, polarized, attached to a basement membrane, and avascular.
Classify by the number of layers and the shape of the most superficial cells, not the basal cells.
Endothelium lines blood and lymph vessels; mesothelium lines serous cavities.
Pseudostratified epithelium has one layer because every cell reaches the basement membrane.
Urothelial umbrella cells may be binucleate and have specialized apical plaques.

traps.wrong: Nuclei at several levels prove the epithelium is stratified.
traps.right: In pseudostratified epithelium, unequal cell height creates staggered nuclei even though all cells touch the basement membrane.

traps.wrong: Stratified epithelia are named by their deepest cells.
traps.right: They are named by the shape of the surface cells.

recognition: Very flat cells with flattened nuclei form simple squamous epithelium.
Cilia, goblet cells, and staggered nuclei strongly suggest respiratory pseudostratified epithelium.
Rounded dome-shaped surface cells identify relaxed urothelium.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 4; TUMS EPITHELIAL TISSUE deck, pages 3-7 and 28-38.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Apical, lateral, basal: build the epithelial cell
lessons.subtitle: Junction order, surface specializations, basement membrane, and gland secretion

visual.caption: From apex to base, specializations control absorption, sealing, adhesion, communication, and attachment.

items.label: Apical surface
items.detail: Microvilli and stereocilia have actin cores; motile cilia have 9+2 microtubules.

items.label: Tight junction
items.detail: The most apical junction seals the paracellular pathway and helps preserve polarity.

items.label: Adherens and desmosome
items.detail: Adherens junctions anchor actin belts; desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments at spot welds.

items.label: Gap junction
items.detail: Connexon channels pass ions and small molecules directly between adjacent cells.

items.label: Basal surface
items.detail: Hemidesmosomes bind intermediate filaments to basal lamina; focal adhesions link actin to ECM.

items.label: Gland output
items.detail: Merocrine uses exocytosis, apocrine sheds apical cytoplasm, and holocrine releases whole dying cells.

essentials: The basal lamina contains type IV collagen and laminin; reticular lamina adds connective-tissue components.
Microvilli increase absorptive surface area; cilia move material over the epithelium.
Exocrine glands retain ducts; endocrine glands are ductless and release products toward capillaries.
Goblet cells are unicellular exocrine glands that release mucin by merocrine secretion.
Myoepithelial cells contract around secretory units and small ducts to aid product expulsion.

traps.wrong: A hemidesmosome joins two epithelial cells.
traps.right: A desmosome joins cell to cell; a hemidesmosome anchors cell to basal lamina.

traps.wrong: Stereocilia are exceptionally long motile cilia.
traps.right: They are long, nonmotile, actin-based microvilli.

recognition: A fuzzy apical brush border is densely packed microvilli.
A terminal bar by light microscopy represents the apical junctional complex.
Pale goblet-shaped cells between columnar cells are mucin-filled goblet cells.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 4; TUMS EPITHELIAL TISSUE deck, pages 9-26 and 39-45.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Cells plus matrix make connective tissue
lessons.subtitle: Identify resident and wandering cells, fiber types, and ground substance

visual.caption: The balance of cells, fibers, and hydrated ground substance determines the tissue's job.

items.label: Fibroblast
items.detail: The principal ECM-producing cell; active cells are plump and basophilic, while fibrocytes are smaller and darker.

items.label: Immune cells
items.detail: Macrophages phagocytose and present antigen; mast cells release inflammatory mediators; plasma cells secrete antibody.

items.label: Type I collagen
items.detail: Thick eosinophilic bundles resist tension in tendon, dermis, bone, and fibrocartilage.

items.label: Type III reticular fibers
items.detail: Thin branching argyrophilic fibers form supportive networks in marrow and lymphoid organs.

items.label: Elastic fibers
items.detail: Elastin plus fibrillin permits stretch and recoil in large arteries, lung, and elastic ligaments.

items.label: Ground substance
items.detail: Hydrated GAGs, proteoglycans, and adhesive glycoproteins support diffusion and resist compression.

essentials: Loose connective tissue has many cells, abundant ground substance, and loosely arranged fibers beneath epithelia.
Dense regular connective tissue has parallel collagen for one-direction tension; dense irregular tissue has interwoven bundles for multidirectional stress.
Plasma cells have eccentric clock-face nuclei and a pale perinuclear Golgi hof.
Mast-cell granules show metachromasia and contain histamine, heparin, proteases, and other mediators.
Type IV collagen forms sheet-like basal lamina networks rather than visible fibers or bundles.

traps.wrong: Reticular fibers are a separate collagen-free fiber family.
traps.right: They are mainly type III collagen arranged as delicate branching networks.

traps.wrong: A plasma cell's pale juxtanuclear area is its nucleus.
traps.right: It is the prominent Golgi apparatus adjacent to an eccentric nucleus.

recognition: Parallel wavy collagen with rows of flattened nuclei suggests tendon.
Irregular thick collagen bundles in many directions suggest dermis.
A delicate black branching network on silver stain identifies reticular fibers.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 5; TUMS The Connective Tissue deck, pages 2-32.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: White stores; brown burns
lessons.subtitle: Two adipocytes with different architecture, blood supply, and physiology

visual.caption: Lipid-droplet architecture reveals whether the cell is optimized for storage or heat generation.

items.label: White adipocyte
items.detail: One giant lipid droplet pushes a flattened nucleus to the edge; sparse cytoplasm forms a signet-ring profile.

items.label: White functions
items.detail: Stores triglyceride, cushions and insulates, and secretes adipokines including leptin and adiponectin.

items.label: Brown adipocyte
items.detail: Many small lipid droplets surround a more central nucleus; abundant mitochondria and capillaries make the tissue brown.

items.label: Brown function
items.detail: Sympathetic stimulation releases fatty acids; UCP1 uncouples oxidative phosphorylation so energy becomes heat.

items.label: Mobilization
items.detail: Catecholamines promote lipolysis; insulin favors glucose uptake and triglyceride storage.

essentials: Routine processing dissolves stored lipid, leaving a large optically empty space in white adipocytes.
Each white adipocyte is supported by reticular fibers and a basal lamina.
Brown fat is especially important in newborn thermogenesis and persists in smaller adult depots.
UCP1 is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and dissipates the proton gradient.
Adipose tissue is highly vascular because lipid storage, release, and endocrine signaling depend on blood flow.

traps.wrong: Brown fat makes ATP more efficiently than white fat.
traps.right: UCP1 uncouples respiration, decreasing ATP capture and releasing energy as heat.

traps.wrong: The empty center of a white adipocyte is a vacuole filled with water.
traps.right: It is the site of a lipid droplet extracted during routine preparation.

recognition: Large clear signet-ring cells with peripheral nuclei are white adipocytes.
Smaller eosinophilic cells with central nuclei and many droplets are brown adipocytes.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 6, Adipose Tissue.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Recognize cartilage by its matrix and fibers
lessons.subtitle: Hyaline, elastic, and fibrocartilage plus appositional and interstitial growth

visual.caption: All cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae; the visible fibers, cell arrangement, and perichondrium separate the types.

items.label: Hyaline
items.detail: Glassy type II collagen matrix with isogenous groups; perichondrium is present except at articular surfaces and growth plates.

items.label: Elastic
items.detail: Hyaline-like cartilage with a conspicuous elastic-fiber network and perichondrium; found in pinna and epiglottis.

items.label: Fibrocartilage
items.detail: Rows of chondrocytes between thick type I collagen bundles; no perichondrium; resists compression and tension.

items.label: Interstitial growth
items.detail: Chondrocytes divide within existing matrix to form isogenous groups and expand from within.

items.label: Appositional growth
items.detail: Perichondrial progenitors become chondroblasts and add new matrix at the surface.

essentials: Cartilage is avascular; nutrients diffuse through the hydrated matrix from perichondrium or synovial fluid.
Chondroblasts secrete matrix at the periphery; mature chondrocytes occupy lacunae.
Territorial matrix around lacunae is more basophilic because it contains more sulfated GAGs.
Hyaline cartilage matrix contains type II collagen fibrils that are usually not individually visible on H&E.
Fibrocartilage combines dense connective tissue with cartilage and therefore lacks perichondrium.

traps.wrong: Every cartilage surface is covered by perichondrium.
traps.right: Articular hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage lack perichondrium.

traps.wrong: A visible thick collagen bundle indicates hyaline cartilage.
traps.right: Thick type I bundles with chondrocyte rows indicate fibrocartilage.

recognition: Glassy matrix with round lacunae and isogenous groups indicates hyaline cartilage.
A dense network of dark branching fibers around lacunae indicates elastic cartilage.
Parallel eosinophilic collagen bundles interrupted by rows of lacunae indicate fibrocartilage.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 7; TUMS BONE&JOINT TISSUE deck, pages 2-16.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Bone is a living lamellar map
lessons.subtitle: Cells, matrix, compact osteons, spongy trabeculae, and remodeling surfaces

visual.caption: Cell shape and position reveal whether bone is being formed, maintained, or resorbed.

items.label: Osteoblast
items.detail: A cuboidal surface cell that secretes type I collagen-rich osteoid and promotes mineralization.

items.label: Osteocyte
items.detail: A former osteoblast trapped in a lacuna; processes communicate through canaliculi and sense mechanical load.

items.label: Osteoclast
items.detail: A large multinucleated monocyte-derived cell in a Howship lacuna; ruffled border acidifies and digests bone.

items.label: Compact bone
items.detail: Osteons surround longitudinal Haversian canals; transverse Volkmann canals connect vascular channels.

items.label: Spongy bone
items.detail: Branching lamellar trabeculae surround marrow spaces and usually lack complete osteons.

essentials: Organic osteoid is mainly type I collagen and ground substance; hydroxyapatite supplies mineral hardness.
Osteoblasts may become osteocytes, bone-lining cells, or undergo apoptosis.
Osteoclasts arise by fusion of monocyte-macrophage precursors, not from osteoblasts.
Periosteum covers external bone except articular surfaces; endosteum lines internal bone surfaces.
Interstitial lamellae are remnants of old osteons left after remodeling.

traps.wrong: Volkmann canals are surrounded by concentric lamellae like osteons.
traps.right: They cross lamellae to connect canals and are not the central axis of an osteon.

traps.wrong: Osteoclasts are multinucleated osteoblasts.
traps.right: They are hematopoietic monocyte-lineage cells specialized for resorption.

recognition: Concentric rings around a central canal identify an osteon.
A huge multinucleated cell on a scalloped bone surface is an osteoclast.
Branching bony plates enclosing marrow spaces identify trabecular bone.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 8; TUMS BONE&JOINT TISSUE deck, pages 17-33.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.topic: Bone formation, growth, repair, and joints
lessons.title: Two routes build bone; one plate lengthens it
lessons.subtitle: Intramembranous versus endochondral ossification, growth-plate zones, remodeling, and synovium

visual.caption: Bone is always laid down by osteoblasts; the difference is whether it begins in mesenchyme or on a cartilage scaffold.

items.label: Intramembranous
items.detail: Mesenchymal cells become osteoblasts directly, form osteoid spicules, and build woven then lamellar bone.

items.label: Endochondral
items.detail: A hyaline cartilage model grows, calcifies, is invaded by vessels, and is replaced by bone.

items.label: Growth plate order
items.detail: From epiphysis to diaphysis: reserve, proliferation, hypertrophy, calcification, then ossification.

items.label: Remodeling and repair
items.detail: Osteoclast cutting cones resorb; vessels and osteoblasts follow to create new lamellar bone.

items.label: Synovial joint
items.detail: Hyaline articular cartilage faces a fluid cavity; a fibrous capsule and vascular synovial lining enclose it.

essentials: Flat skull bones develop mainly by intramembranous ossification; most long bones develop endochondrally.
Articular cartilage lacks perichondrium and receives nutrients from synovial fluid.
Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-like; type B synoviocytes synthesize hyaluronan and other fluid components.
Woven bone is formed rapidly with irregular collagen; remodeling replaces it with organized lamellar bone.
Fracture repair progresses through hematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard bony callus, then remodeling.

traps.wrong: Endochondral ossification turns chondrocytes directly into osteocytes.
traps.right: Most cartilage calcifies and is removed; osteoblasts deposit bone on remaining calcified cartilage spicules.

traps.wrong: Intramembranous bone has no cartilage anywhere in the mature skeleton.
traps.right: The name describes the developmental route, not every mature neighboring structure.

recognition: Columns of flattened dividing chondrocytes identify the proliferative growth-plate zone.
Large pale lacunae identify hypertrophic cartilage.
A cavity between smooth articular cartilage surfaces identifies a synovial joint.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 8; TUMS BONE&JOINT TISSUE deck, pages 34-55.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Identify muscle before answering its physiology
lessons.subtitle: Cell shape, nuclei, striations, junctions, and regenerative capacity

visual.caption: Nuclear position and cell outline are the fastest identifiers; striations and junctions confirm.

items.label: Skeletal
items.detail: Long unbranched multinucleated fibers, peripheral nuclei, strong striations, and no cell-to-cell junctional discs.

items.label: Cardiac
items.detail: Short branched striated cells with one or two central nuclei and dark intercalated discs.

items.label: Smooth
items.detail: Spindle cells with one central cigar-shaped nucleus, no visible striations, and actin anchored to dense bodies.

items.label: Membrane-SR unit
items.detail: Skeletal muscle has triads at A-I junctions; cardiac muscle has diads near Z lines; smooth muscle uses caveolae and sparse SR.

items.label: Repair
items.detail: Skeletal satellite cells permit limited repair, cardiac repair is minimal and fibrotic, smooth muscle can divide and hypertrophy.

essentials: Sarcomeres run from Z disc to Z disc; A-band length stays constant during contraction while I band and H zone shorten.
Intercalated discs combine fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions for mechanical and electrical coupling.
Smooth-muscle contraction uses calcium-calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase rather than troponin.
Endomysium surrounds individual muscle cells, perimysium surrounds fascicles, and epimysium surrounds the entire muscle.
Cardiac cells have abundant mitochondria and a rich capillary supply.

traps.wrong: A central nucleus excludes striated muscle.
traps.right: Cardiac muscle is striated and usually has a central nucleus.

traps.wrong: Smooth muscle lacks organized actin and myosin because it has no striations.
traps.right: It has both filaments, but they are arranged obliquely around dense bodies rather than in sarcomeres.

recognition: Peripheral nuclei beneath the sarcolemma identify skeletal muscle.
Branching fibers and transverse dark intercalated discs identify cardiac muscle.
Bundles of spindle cells with elongated central nuclei identify smooth muscle.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 10; TUMS skeletal and smooth muscle teacher decks.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Neuron, myelin, and glia as one working circuit
lessons.subtitle: Recognize the conducting cell, its support cells, and its peripheral coverings

visual.caption: The neuron conducts; glia maintain its chemical, metabolic, immune, and insulating environment.

items.label: Neuron
items.detail: Soma and dendrites receive; the axon hillock initiates output; the axon conducts to terminals.

items.label: CNS support
items.detail: Astrocytes regulate the environment and aid the blood-brain barrier; microglia phagocytose; ependymal cells line ventricles.

items.label: Myelin
items.detail: One oligodendrocyte myelinates segments on multiple CNS axons; one Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one PNS axon.

items.label: Peripheral nerve
items.detail: Endoneurium surrounds fibers, perineurium encloses fascicles and forms a barrier, epineurium encloses the nerve.

items.label: Ganglia
items.detail: Sensory ganglia have large neurons in orderly clusters with continuous satellite-cell rings; autonomic ganglia are more irregular.

essentials: Nissl substance is RER and free polyribosomes in soma and dendrites; it is absent from the axon hillock and axon.
Fast axonal transport uses microtubules: kinesin is mainly anterograde and dynein retrograde.
Nodes of Ranvier interrupt myelin and concentrate ion channels for saltatory conduction.
The PNS has greater regenerative potential because Schwann cells and endoneurial tubes guide axonal sprouts.
Synapses are asymmetric chemical junctions unless gap junctions form an electrical synapse.

traps.wrong: Schwann cells make all nervous-system myelin.
traps.right: Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.

traps.wrong: Nissl substance extends through the axon.
traps.right: The axon hillock and axon lack RER and therefore lack Nissl substance.

recognition: A large pale soma with a prominent nucleolus and basophilic clumps is a neuron.
A honeycomb of clear rings in nerve cross-section represents myelinated fibers after lipid extraction.
A complete ring of satellite cells around each large neuron favors a sensory ganglion.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 9; TUMS NERVOUS TISSUE MEDICINE deck, slides 5-70.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Read the smear: erythrocytes and platelets
lessons.subtitle: Size anchors, shape, lifespan, and the platelet response to vessel injury

visual.caption: Use the 7.5-micrometer erythrocyte as the ruler for every other cell in a blood smear.

items.label: Erythrocyte
items.detail: An anucleate biconcave disc about 7.5 micrometers wide with central pallor occupying roughly one-third of its diameter.

items.label: Reticulocyte
items.detail: A slightly larger young RBC with residual ribosomal RNA, visible as a reticulum using supravital stain.

items.label: Platelet
items.detail: A 2-4 micrometer anucleate megakaryocyte fragment with pale peripheral hyalomere and darker central granulomere.

items.label: Adhesion
items.detail: Vessel injury exposes collagen; von Willebrand factor links collagen to platelet GPIb.

items.label: Aggregation
items.detail: Activation changes shape and releases granules; fibrinogen bridges platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors.

essentials: Mature erythrocytes lack nucleus and organelles, maximizing hemoglobin space but preventing repair or protein synthesis.
Their spectrin-actin membrane skeleton permits deformation through narrow capillaries.
Old RBCs are removed mainly by macrophages in spleen, liver, and marrow after about 120 days.
Platelet alpha granules contain adhesive and repair proteins; dense granules contain ADP, calcium, and serotonin.
A platelet's marginal microtubule bundle maintains its resting discoid shape.

traps.wrong: A reticulocyte has a small residual nucleus.
traps.right: It is already anucleate; only residual ribosomal RNA remains.

traps.wrong: GPIIb/IIIa mediates initial adhesion to exposed collagen through vWF.
traps.right: GPIb mediates vWF-dependent adhesion; GPIIb/IIIa mediates fibrinogen-dependent aggregation.

recognition: Numerous uniform pink discs with central pallor are erythrocytes.
Very small purple granular fragments between RBCs are platelets.
Diffuse bluish polychromasia in a young RBC suggests a reticulocyte.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 12; TUMS Blood& HEM deck, pages 3-15 and 31-38.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Identify every leukocyte in seconds
lessons.subtitle: Nuclear silhouette, granule color, relative size, and core function

visual.caption: Start with nucleus shape, then confirm with granule color and cell size.

items.label: Neutrophil
items.detail: Most common WBC; 3-5 nuclear lobes with pale fine granules; rapid phagocyte in acute inflammation.

items.label: Eosinophil
items.detail: Bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules; attacks parasites and modulates allergy.

items.label: Basophil
items.detail: Coarse dark blue-purple granules often obscure an S-shaped nucleus; IgE-linked mediator release.

items.label: Lymphocyte
items.detail: Usually small with a dense round nucleus and thin pale rim of cytoplasm; adaptive immunity or NK function.

items.label: Monocyte
items.detail: Largest circulating WBC with kidney-shaped pale nucleus and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm; macrophage precursor.

essentials: Neutrophil azurophilic granules are lysosome-like; specific granules contain antimicrobial proteins and enzymes.
Eosinophil granule cores contain major basic protein toxic to helminths.
Basophils resemble mast cells functionally but are distinct circulating cells.
Small lymphocytes can look only slightly larger than RBCs; monocytes are usually the largest cells in a normal smear.
Leukocytes leave postcapillary venules through rolling, adhesion, and diapedesis.

traps.wrong: A bilobed nucleus alone identifies a basophil.
traps.right: Eosinophils also have bilobed nuclei; use orange-red versus dark purple granules.

traps.wrong: Lymphocytes lack cytoplasm.
traps.right: Small lymphocytes have a narrow rim that may be hard to see, but it is present.

recognition: Three to five connected nuclear lobes identify a neutrophil.
Large orange-red granules identify an eosinophil.
A folded kidney-shaped nucleus with abundant gray cytoplasm identifies a monocyte.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 12; TUMS Blood& HEM deck, pages 16-30.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: One stem cell, two major lineages
lessons.subtitle: Marrow organization and the erythroid, granulocytic, lymphoid, monocytic, and megakaryocytic branches

visual.caption: A self-renewing stem cell generates committed progenitors that progressively restrict lineage choice.

items.label: HSC
items.detail: A rare multipotent, self-renewing marrow cell gives rise to common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors.

items.label: Myeloid branch
items.detail: Produces erythrocytes, megakaryocytes and platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes.

items.label: Lymphoid branch
items.detail: Produces B cells, T cells, and NK cells; T-cell precursors complete maturation in thymus.

items.label: Marrow niche
items.detail: Developing cells lie in cords between sinusoidal capillaries supported by reticular stromal cells and macrophages.

items.label: Growth signals
items.detail: EPO favors erythroid survival, thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes, and CSFs guide granulocyte-monocyte production.

essentials: Red marrow is hematopoietically active; yellow marrow is adipocyte-rich but can revert toward red marrow under severe demand.
Megakaryocytes become polyploid by endomitosis and extend proplatelets through sinusoidal endothelium.
Granulocytes develop from myeloblast through promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band cell, then mature cell.
The myelocyte is the last granulocytic stage capable of mitosis and the first stage with lineage-specific granules.
Marrow macrophages remove extruded erythroblast nuclei and recycle iron.

traps.wrong: Platelets are complete cells released by mitosis of megakaryocytes.
traps.right: They are cytoplasmic fragments shed from polyploid megakaryocytes.

traps.wrong: All lymphocyte maturation occurs in bone marrow.
traps.right: B cells mature in marrow; T-cell precursors migrate to thymus.

recognition: A giant multilobed marrow cell beside a sinusoid is a megakaryocyte.
Hematopoietic cords packed with cells at many stages distinguish red marrow from adipocyte-dominant yellow marrow.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 13; TUMS Blood& HEM deck, pages 43-55.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Erythropoiesis is a color-and-size sequence
lessons.subtitle: Track hemoglobin, ribosomes, nuclear condensation, and enucleation stage by stage

visual.caption: Cells become smaller and pinker while the nucleus condenses and is eventually expelled.

items.label: Proerythroblast
items.detail: Large cell, fine chromatin, nucleoli, and strongly basophilic cytoplasm from abundant ribosomes.

items.label: Basophilic erythroblast
items.detail: Smaller, no visible nucleoli, deeply basophilic cytoplasm; hemoglobin synthesis begins on abundant polyribosomes.

items.label: Polychromatophilic erythroblast
items.detail: Both blue ribosomal RNA and pink hemoglobin are abundant, creating gray-lilac cytoplasm; nucleus is more condensed.

items.label: Orthochromatophilic erythroblast
items.detail: Small cell with eosinophilic hemoglobin-rich cytoplasm and a pyknotic nucleus that is then expelled.

items.label: Reticulocyte to RBC
items.detail: An anucleate reticulocyte retains slight RNA polychromasia, enters blood, and matures in about one day.

essentials: Hemoglobin synthesis begins in the basophilic erythroblast, not the later orthochromatophilic stage.
Across the sequence, cell size and nuclear size decrease, chromatin condenses, and cytoplasm shifts from blue to pink.
Erythroblastic islands consist of developing erythroid cells around a central macrophage.
Erythropoietin from the kidney rises in response to hypoxia and supports erythroid progenitor survival.
Reticulocytes are normally a small fraction of circulating RBCs; an increased count indicates marrow response.

traps.wrong: Hemoglobin first appears when the cytoplasm becomes fully pink.
traps.right: Synthesis begins earlier in basophilic erythroblasts; pink staining becomes obvious later as hemoglobin accumulates.

traps.wrong: The reticulocyte ejects its nucleus in circulation.
traps.right: The orthochromatophilic erythroblast ejects the nucleus in marrow; the reticulocyte is already anucleate.

recognition: Deep blue cytoplasm with condensed nucleus indicates a basophilic erythroblast.
Gray-lilac cytoplasm indicates the mixed RNA and hemoglobin of a polychromatophilic erythroblast.
Pink cytoplasm around a tiny dense nucleus indicates an orthochromatophilic erythroblast.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 13, Figure 13-6 and erythropoiesis text; TUMS Blood& HEM deck.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Climb the epidermis from stem cell to keratin
lessons.subtitle: Strata, epidermal cell types, dermis, thick-versus-thin skin, and sensory structures

visual.caption: From deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum only in thick skin, then corneum.

items.label: Basale
items.detail: One mitotically active row attached to basal lamina; contains stem keratinocytes, melanocytes, and Merkel cells.

items.label: Spinosum
items.detail: Several layers linked by many desmosomes; shrinkage makes intercellular spines visible.

items.label: Granulosum
items.detail: Flattening cells contain basophilic keratohyalin granules and release lipid-rich lamellar bodies for the water barrier.

items.label: Lucidum
items.detail: A thin pale layer of anucleate cells seen only in thick skin.

items.label: Corneum
items.detail: Flattened dead keratin-filled squames form the surface mechanical barrier.

items.label: Dermis
items.detail: Superficial papillary loose CT supports capillaries and Meissner corpuscles; deeper reticular dense irregular CT contains appendages and Pacinian corpuscles.

essentials: Melanocytes derive from neural crest and transfer melanin to keratinocytes; skin color differences mainly reflect melanin production and degradation, not melanocyte number.
Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting dendritic cells, especially in stratum spinosum.
Merkel cells associate with sensory nerve endings in the basal layer for fine touch.
Thick skin has a very thick epidermis, lucidum, and eccrine glands but no hair follicles or sebaceous glands.
Meissner corpuscles are superficial and touch-sensitive; Pacinian corpuscles are deep onion-like pressure and vibration receptors.

traps.wrong: Melanocytes form desmosomes with surrounding keratinocytes.
traps.right: They extend processes and transfer melanosomes but do not form the usual desmosomal attachments with keratinocytes.

traps.wrong: Stratum lucidum is present wherever epidermis is thin and transparent.
traps.right: It is a feature of thick skin on palms and soles.

recognition: A very thick corneum, visible lucidum, and absence of hair identify thick skin.
An onion-like encapsulated receptor deep in dermis or hypodermis is a Pacinian corpuscle.
A small oval receptor in a dermal papilla is a Meissner corpuscle.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 18; TUMS SKIN deck, slides 2-24 and 32.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Decode every skin receptor by depth, stimulus, and adaptation
lessons.subtitle: Free endings, Merkel, Meissner, Pacinian, Ruffini, Krause, and root-hair plexuses on one comparison slide

visual.caption: Solve receptor questions in three passes: identify the stimulus, place the receptor by depth, then check whether the signal is sustained or rapidly changing.

items.label: Free nerve endings
items.detail: Unencapsulated fibers in papillary dermis that can enter lower epidermis; detect pain, hot or cold extremes, itching, and some crude touch.

items.label: Merkel tactile disc
items.detail: Unencapsulated Merkel cell-neurite complex in stratum basale; a tonic receptor for sustained light touch, edges, form, and texture.

items.label: Meissner corpuscle
items.detail: Small encapsulated oval in dermal papillae of glabrous skin; phasic light-touch and low-frequency deformation receptor, dense in fingertips.

items.label: Pacinian corpuscle
items.detail: Large encapsulated receptor in deep reticular dermis or hypodermis; concentric lamellae amplify coarse pressure and high-frequency vibration.

items.label: Ruffini corpuscle
items.detail: Fusiform collagenous capsule anchored to connective tissue; deformation signals skin stretch, tension, and twisting or torque.

items.label: Krause end bulb
items.detail: Small simple encapsulated ovoid receptor, emphasized in penile and clitoral skin; Junqueira assigns it low-frequency vibration or movement.

items.label: Root-hair plexus
items.detail: Unencapsulated sensory web around the base of a hair follicle in reticular dermis; bending the hair produces light-touch input.

essentials: The fastest discriminator is modality: pain, temperature, and itch mean free endings; sustained texture means Merkel; flutter or light deformation means Meissner; deep pressure or high-frequency vibration means Pacinian.
Depth is the visual map: Merkel and free endings are epidermal or very superficial, Meissner is in a dermal papilla, and Pacinian is deep in reticular dermis or hypodermis.
Unencapsulated receptors are free endings, Merkel tactile discs, and root-hair plexuses; Meissner, Pacinian, Ruffini, and Krause receptors are encapsulated.
For adaptation, memorize Merkel as tonic and Meissner/Pacinian as phasic. In physiology classifications Ruffini endings are commonly described as slowly adapting stretch receptors.
Junqueira links fingertip two-point discrimination to Meissner corpuscle density and notes that this density declines during adult life.
Meissner corpuscles are numerous in fingertips, palms, and soles; root-hair plexuses require hairy skin and therefore are absent from glabrous palms and soles.

traps.wrong: Any vibration is Pacinian.
traps.right: High-frequency or deep vibration favors Pacinian; low-frequency superficial deformation favors Meissner, while Junqueira assigns genital low-frequency vibration to Krause bulbs.

traps.wrong: Two-point discrimination is a deep-pressure function, so the answer is Pacinian.
traps.right: Fine superficial spatial discrimination at the fingertip tracks dense Meissner corpuscles; Junqueira explicitly connects their age-related decline to worsening two-point discrimination.

traps.wrong: All light touch is detected by the same receptor.
traps.right: Sustained texture and edges favor Merkel, changing superficial touch favors Meissner, and movement of a hair favors a root-hair plexus.

traps.wrong: Every receptor that reaches the epidermis has a connective-tissue capsule.
traps.right: Free endings and Merkel-associated tactile discs are unencapsulated; the major encapsulated corpuscles lie in dermis or hypodermis.

recognition: A small pale oval with stacked flattened Schwann cells inside a dermal papilla is a Meissner corpuscle.
A large onion-like body with many concentric lamellae among deep dermal or hypodermal adipocytes is a Pacinian corpuscle.
A fusiform collagenous receptor blending into deep connective tissue favors a Ruffini corpuscle.
Free endings, Merkel complexes, Krause bulbs, and root-hair plexuses are usually difficult to identify in routine H&E sections; use the stated location and modality.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 18, Figures 18-9, 18-11, and 18-12; sensory receptor text on pages 381-383.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Hair, sebaceous, eccrine, or apocrine?
lessons.subtitle: Use duct destination, lumen size, secretion mechanism, and location

visual.caption: Coiled sweat glands look similar; lumen, epithelial height, and where the duct opens are decisive.

items.label: Eccrine gland
items.detail: Small-lumen coiled secretory tubule with clear and dark cells; duct opens directly to surface and supports thermoregulation.

items.label: Apocrine gland
items.detail: Large-lumen coiled gland in axilla, areola, and anogenital skin; duct usually opens into a hair follicle.

items.label: Sebaceous gland
items.detail: Branched acini of pale lipid-filled cells empty holocrine sebum into hair follicles.

items.label: Hair follicle
items.detail: Epidermal invagination surrounds the shaft; matrix cells in the bulb divide around a vascular dermal papilla.

items.label: Arrector pili
items.detail: A small smooth-muscle bundle connects superficial dermis to the follicular sheath.

essentials: Despite its historical name, the human apocrine sweat gland releases most product by merocrine exocytosis.
Eccrine ducts have stratified cuboidal epithelium, a smaller lumen, and no myoepithelial cells in the duct wall.
Myoepithelial cells lie between secretory cells and basal lamina of sweat glands and contract to expel secretion.
Sebaceous glands are absent from thick skin because they are usually associated with hair follicles.
Hair matrix and nail matrix contain proliferating cells that generate hard keratin.

traps.wrong: Any gland beside a hair follicle is apocrine.
traps.right: Sebaceous glands are pale acini; apocrine glands are coiled tubules with a large lumen.

traps.wrong: Eccrine secretory portions and ducts have identical staining.
traps.right: The duct is darker and stratified cuboidal; the secretory portion is paler with a wider lumen.

recognition: Pale foamy acini opening into a follicle identify a sebaceous gland.
A coiled tubule with a very wide lumen near a follicle favors an apocrine gland.
A darker two-layered cuboidal profile within an eccrine coil is its duct.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 18; TUMS SKIN deck, slides 25-30.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: From basal spermatogonium to luminal spermatozoon
lessons.subtitle: Map the seminiferous epithelium, meiosis, Sertoli support, and Leydig endocrine function

visual.caption: Development advances from the basal compartment toward the lumen while Sertoli cells span the entire epithelium.

items.label: Basal spermatogonia
items.detail: Diploid stem and differentiating cells lie directly on the basal lamina and divide mitotically.

items.label: Primary spermatocytes
items.detail: Large cells with coarse threadlike meiotic chromatin cross the Sertoli barrier and spend a long prophase I.

items.label: Secondary spermatocytes
items.detail: Short-lived haploid products of meiosis I rapidly enter meiosis II and are rarely seen.

items.label: Spermatids
items.detail: Small round then elongated haploid cells near the lumen remodel through spermiogenesis without further division.

items.label: Sertoli cell
items.detail: A tall support cell with pale ovoid nucleus and prominent nucleolus; tight junctions create basal and adluminal compartments.

items.label: Leydig cell
items.detail: Eosinophilic steroid-secreting cells in vascular interstitial clusters make testosterone in response to LH.

essentials: The germ-cell order from base to lumen is spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, spermatozoon.
Spermiogenesis transforms spermatids by forming acrosome and flagellum, condensing nucleus, and shedding excess cytoplasm.
Sertoli cells respond mainly to FSH and testosterone, nourish germ cells, phagocytose residual bodies, secrete inhibin, and make androgen-binding protein.
The blood-testis barrier is formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells, not by capillary endothelium alone.
Primary spermatocytes are commonly seen; secondary spermatocytes are rare because meiosis II follows quickly.

traps.wrong: Sertoli cells lie only at the base of the seminiferous epithelium.
traps.right: Their nuclei are basal, but their cytoplasm extends from basal lamina to lumen.

traps.wrong: LH directly stimulates Sertoli cells to make inhibin.
traps.right: LH stimulates Leydig testosterone; FSH acts primarily on Sertoli cells.

recognition: Round tubules with a thick multilayered germinal epithelium and central tails are seminiferous tubules.
Large coarse-chromatin cells above the basal layer are primary spermatocytes.
Clusters of eosinophilic cells between tubules are Leydig cells.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 21, Male Reproductive System.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Follow sperm from testis to urethra
lessons.subtitle: Duct epithelium, smooth muscle, sperm maturation, and accessory-gland fingerprints

visual.caption: The route is straight tubule, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.

items.label: Efferent ductules
items.detail: Alternating tall ciliated and short absorptive cells create a scalloped lumen and reclaim most testicular fluid.

items.label: Epididymis
items.detail: A single highly coiled duct with pseudostratified columnar epithelium and long stereocilia; sperm mature and are stored here.
items.cue: Smooth round lumen full of sperm

items.label: Ductus deferens
items.detail: A small folded lumen is surrounded by an extremely thick three-layer smooth-muscle wall.

items.label: Seminal vesicle
items.detail: A single tortuous gland with labyrinthine mucosal folds and smooth muscle; secretes fructose-rich alkaline fluid.

items.label: Prostate
items.detail: Tubuloalveolar glands lie in fibromuscular stroma around the prostatic urethra; lumina often contain corpora amylacea.

items.label: Bulbourethral gland
items.detail: Mucous tubuloalveolar glands in skeletal muscle release lubricating pre-ejaculate into the spongy urethra.

essentials: Epididymal stereocilia are long actin-based microvilli, not motile cilia.
Sperm acquire motility competence during epididymal passage but are not yet capable of fertilization until capacitation in the female tract.
Ductus deferens smooth muscle propels sperm during ejaculation.
Seminal-vesicle mucosa is highly folded but does not contain separate glandular acini.
Corpora amylacea are often laminated eosinophilic prostatic concretions that become more common with age.

traps.wrong: The seminal vesicle stores sperm because its name includes vesicle.
traps.right: Sperm are stored mainly in epididymis; seminal vesicles contribute secretory fluid.

traps.wrong: Both epididymis and efferent ductules have a scalloped lumen.
traps.right: Alternating epithelial heights make efferent ductules scalloped; epididymis has a more even epithelial border.

recognition: Alternating tall and short cells with a scalloped lumen identify efferent ductules.
Long stereocilia and a sperm-filled lumen identify epididymis.
A very thick muscular wall around a narrow folded lumen identifies ductus deferens.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 21, Male Reproductive System.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Follicles grow from cortex to ovulation
lessons.subtitle: Oocyte status, granulosa layers, zona pellucida, theca, antrum, and corpus luteum

visual.caption: Follicle stage is named by the surrounding follicular tissue, not by a change in the oocyte's meiotic stage.

items.label: Primordial
items.detail: A primary oocyte arrested in prophase I is surrounded by one layer of flattened follicular cells in ovarian cortex.

items.label: Primary
items.detail: Follicular cells become cuboidal granulosa, then multilayered; zona pellucida appears around the growing oocyte.

items.label: Secondary/antral
items.detail: Fluid spaces merge into an antrum; stromal theca differentiates into steroidogenic interna and fibrous externa.

items.label: Mature/Graafian
items.detail: A huge antrum displaces the oocyte to a cumulus oophorus; corona radiata directly surrounds the zona pellucida.

items.label: Corpus luteum
items.detail: After ovulation, granulosa lutein and theca lutein cells form a vascular progesterone-secreting endocrine gland.

items.label: Corpus albicans
items.detail: Without sustained hCG, luteal cells regress and are replaced by a hyalinized collagen scar.

essentials: The oocyte remains a primary oocyte through most follicular growth and completes meiosis I just before ovulation.
The ovulated cell is a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II; meiosis II finishes only after fertilization.
Granulosa cells convert theca-derived androgens to estrogens under FSH stimulation.
Theca interna is vascular and steroidogenic; granulosa is initially avascular and separated from theca by a basal lamina.
Follicular atresia can occur at any stage and greatly exceeds the number of ovulated follicles.

traps.wrong: A primary follicle contains a secondary oocyte.
traps.right: Primary refers to follicle morphology; its oocyte is still primary and arrested in prophase I.

traps.wrong: The corona radiata is the same as the cumulus oophorus.
traps.right: Corona radiata is the innermost granulosa layer around the zona; cumulus is the larger mound attaching the oocyte to the follicle wall.

recognition: A tiny cortical oocyte with flattened surrounding cells is a primordial follicle.
A fluid-filled antrum establishes an antral follicle.
Large pale polygonal cells in folded, highly vascular tissue identify corpus luteum.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 22, Female Reproductive System.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Tube transport and the uterine cycle
lessons.subtitle: Recognize uterine tube, proliferative endometrium, secretory endometrium, and menstruation

visual.caption: Estrogen rebuilds a straight-gland endometrium; progesterone converts it into a coiled, secretory implantation bed.

items.label: Uterine tube
items.detail: Highly branched mucosal folds have ciliated and secretory simple columnar cells; fertilization usually occurs in ampulla.

items.label: Menstrual phase
items.detail: Loss of progesterone causes spiral-artery constriction and shedding of stratum functionale; basale remains.

items.label: Proliferative phase
items.detail: Estrogen rebuilds functionale; glands are relatively straight and narrow with mitoses.

items.label: Early secretory phase
items.detail: After ovulation, progesterone causes subnuclear glycogen vacuoles in glandular cells.

items.label: Mid-secretory phase
items.detail: Glands become saw-toothed and secrete into the lumen; stroma becomes edematous and predecidual.

items.label: Myometrium
items.detail: Interwoven smooth-muscle bundles hypertrophy greatly during pregnancy and contract at birth.

essentials: The uterine tube mucosa has elaborate folds but no true glands and no distinct submucosa.
Cilia beat toward the uterus; secretory peg cells support gametes and the early embryo.
Stratum functionale is hormone-responsive and shed; stratum basale regenerates it after menstruation.
Straight glands indicate proliferative endometrium, while corkscrew or saw-toothed glands indicate secretory endometrium.
Spiral arteries supply functionale; straighter arteries remain in basale.

traps.wrong: The most folded uterine tube segment is the intramural part.
traps.right: The ampulla has an especially complex folded mucosa and is the usual fertilization site.

traps.wrong: All endometrium is lost during normal menstruation.
traps.right: The functionale is shed, while basale remains to regenerate the lining.

recognition: A star-like lumen crowded by branching folds but lacking glands suggests uterine tube.
Straight tubular glands with frequent mitoses indicate proliferative endometrium.
Saw-toothed glands with luminal secretion and edematous stroma indicate secretory endometrium.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 22, Female Reproductive System.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Recognize cervix, vagina, and mammary gland
lessons.subtitle: Three common practical stations distinguished by epithelium, glands, and hormonal state

visual.caption: Surface epithelium identifies cervix and vagina; lobule-to-stroma ratio identifies mammary activity.

items.label: Endocervix
items.detail: Mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium forms deep branched cervical glands.

items.label: Ectocervix
items.detail: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium faces the vagina; its junction with endocervix is the transformation zone.

items.label: Vagina
items.detail: A folded nonkeratinized stratified squamous mucosa overlies elastic CT and smooth muscle; there are no mucosal glands.

items.label: Inactive mammary gland
items.detail: Sparse small ducts lie in abundant dense and adipose stroma with few developed secretory alveoli.

items.label: Lactating mammary gland
items.detail: Numerous enlarged secretory alveoli fill lobules, stroma is reduced, and lumina contain milk product.

items.label: Milk secretion
items.detail: Protein is released merocrinely; lipid droplets are released with apical cytoplasm by an apocrine mechanism.

essentials: The cervical transformation zone is clinically important because metaplasia and most cervical neoplasia arise there.
Vaginal epithelial glycogen supports lactobacilli, which help maintain an acidic environment.
Vaginal lubrication comes mainly from cervical mucus and transudate because the vaginal mucosa lacks glands.
Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis; oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells for milk ejection.
Mammary alveoli are best developed during pregnancy and lactation.

traps.wrong: Mucus in the vagina proves that vaginal glands are present.
traps.right: The vaginal wall has no glands; cervical mucus and vascular transudate supply fluid.

traps.wrong: All milk components use apocrine secretion.
traps.right: Milk protein is merocrine; milk lipid uses apocrine-like budding.

recognition: A sharp meeting of simple columnar and stratified squamous epithelia identifies the cervical transformation zone.
Thick nonkeratinized squamous epithelium with no glands favors vagina.
Closely packed milk-filled alveoli with little stroma identify lactating mammary gland.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 22, Female Reproductive System.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Recognize gut and urinary specimens at low power
lessons.subtitle: Start with wall organization, surface shape, glands, and the lining epithelium

visual.caption: Digestive organs are identified by mucosal architecture; urinary organs by renal corpuscles, tubule profiles, or urothelium.

items.label: Esophagus and stomach
items.detail: Esophagus has nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium and submucosal glands; stomach has pits and glands but no villi.

items.label: Small intestine
items.detail: Villi plus crypts identify small intestine: duodenum has Brunner glands, jejunum tall folds, ileum Peyer patches.

items.label: Colon
items.detail: Straight closely packed crypts with abundant goblet cells and no villi produce a flat luminal surface.

items.label: Renal cortex
items.detail: Renal corpuscles occur only in cortex. PCT has eosinophilic cells and a fuzzy small lumen; DCT has a clearer wider lumen.

items.label: Renal medulla
items.detail: Parallel collecting ducts, loops of Henle, and capillaries dominate; renal corpuscles are absent.

items.label: Ureter and bladder
items.detail: Both have urothelium. Ureter has a folded star-shaped lumen and thick muscle; bladder has broad rugae and detrusor bundles.

essentials: The GI wall usually follows mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, then serosa or adventitia.
A villus is a mucosal projection with a connective-tissue core; a crypt is an epithelial invagination.
Brush borders make PCT lumina look fuzzy, while DCT lumina are cleaner and their cells appear smaller.
Podocyte nuclei lie on glomerular capillaries; the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is simple squamous.
Urothelial umbrella cells change shape with distension while preserving a tight urine barrier.

traps.wrong: Any intestinal section with many goblet cells is ileum.
traps.right: Ileum needs villi plus large aggregated lymphoid nodules; colon has many goblet cells but no villi.

traps.wrong: Every round renal tubule with a small lumen is PCT.
traps.right: Confirm the eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical brush border; thin limbs and vessels can also have small lumina.

recognition: Villi over pale submucosal Brunner glands identify duodenum.
A flat colonic surface over straight goblet-rich crypts identifies colon.
A capillary tuft within Bowman's space is a renal corpuscle and proves cortex.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapters 15 and 19; practical image-recognition exception only.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Recognize endocrine glands and lymphoid organs
lessons.subtitle: Follicles, cords, zones, lobules, and nodules create distinct low-power fingerprints

visual.caption: Endocrine tissue clusters around capillaries; lymphoid tissue organizes immune cells into compartments and filters lymph or blood.

items.label: Thyroid and parathyroid
items.detail: Thyroid is unique for colloid-filled follicles; parathyroid is a solid corded gland of chief cells with increasing adipocytes after puberty.

items.label: Pituitary and adrenal
items.detail: Anterior pituitary is a mixed dark cellular field; posterior pituitary is pale and fibrous. Adrenal has cortical zones around a central medulla.

items.label: Thymus
items.detail: Lobules have dark cortex, pale medulla, and eosinophilic Hassall corpuscles; lymphoid follicles are absent.

items.label: Lymph node
items.detail: A capsule surrounds cortical follicles, paracortex, and medullary cords and sinuses; afferent lymph enters the convex surface.

items.label: Spleen
items.detail: White pulp lymphoid nodules surround central arteries within red pulp cords and sinusoids; there is no cortex-medulla division.

essentials: Thyroid stores hormone precursor extracellularly in colloid, unlike most endocrine glands.
Adrenal cortex runs glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis from capsule inward; medulla contains chromaffin cells and large veins.
Thymic cortex is darker because it contains densely packed immature T cells.
Lymph nodes filter lymph, while spleen filters blood and removes old erythrocytes.
Spleen central arteries are typically eccentric within white pulp rather than truly central.

traps.wrong: Any dark cortex and pale medulla identify a lymph node.
traps.right: Thymus also has dark cortex and pale medulla; lobulation and Hassall corpuscles identify thymus.

traps.wrong: Splenic white pulp is the pale background of the spleen.
traps.right: White pulp is basophilic lymphoid tissue around arteries; the more extensive background is red pulp.

recognition: Round follicles filled with homogeneous pink colloid identify thyroid.
Concentric eosinophilic Hassall corpuscles identify thymic medulla.
A lymphoid nodule built around a central artery identifies splenic white pulp.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapters 14 and 20; practical image-recognition exception only.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Walk the airway until gas exchange begins
lessons.subtitle: Cartilage, glands, epithelium, smooth muscle, and alveoli mark each branch

visual.caption: As airways narrow, cartilage and glands disappear, epithelium gets lower, and alveoli eventually interrupt the wall.

items.label: Trachea
items.detail: Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells, submucosal seromucous glands, and C-shaped hyaline cartilage.

items.label: Intrapulmonary bronchus
items.detail: Irregular cartilage plates and glands surround a folded mucosa with a continuous smooth-muscle layer.

items.label: Terminal bronchiole
items.detail: No cartilage or glands; simple ciliated cuboidal cells and club cells form a continuous wall with smooth muscle.

items.label: Respiratory bronchiole
items.detail: The cuboidal bronchiolar wall is first interrupted by scattered alveoli, marking the start of gas exchange.

items.label: Alveolar duct and sac
items.detail: Alveoli line almost the entire passage; smooth-muscle knobs mark alveolar openings before clusters end in sacs.

items.label: Alveolar cells
items.detail: Flat type I cells cover most surface; cuboidal type II cells secrete surfactant and replace damaged alveolar epithelium.

essentials: Bronchioles are defined by absence of cartilage and submucosal glands.
Terminal bronchioles are entirely conducting; respiratory bronchioles have alveoli in their walls.
The blood-air barrier is type I cytoplasm, fused basal laminae, and capillary endothelium.
Type II pneumocytes contain lamellar bodies and reduce alveolar surface tension through surfactant.
Alveolar macrophages patrol septa and lumina and may carry particles toward bronchioles or lymphatics.

traps.wrong: Any airway without cartilage is a terminal bronchiole.
traps.right: All bronchioles lack cartilage; alveoli in the wall make it a respiratory bronchiole.

traps.wrong: Type II pneumocytes cover most alveolar surface.
traps.right: They are more numerous than their small surface contribution suggests; thin type I cells cover most surface area.

recognition: A C-shaped cartilage ring and posterior smooth muscle identify trachea.
An airway with no cartilage or glands but an intact wall identifies terminal bronchiole.
Cuboidal cells bulging at alveolar corners suggest type II pneumocytes.

source.label: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 16th ed.
source.detail: Chapter 17; TUMS respiratory practical material and image set; practical image-recognition exception only.

lessons.subject: histology
lessons.title: Orient the eye and inner ear
lessons.subtitle: Retinal layers, cornea, lens, and the sensory epithelia most likely to appear as spotters

visual.caption: For retina, orient from choroid toward vitreous; light and neural information travel in opposite directions.

items.label: Retina outer side
items.detail: Pigmented epithelium lies against choroid, followed by photoreceptor outer segments and the outer nuclear layer.

items.label: Retina inner side
items.detail: Inner nuclear layer, ganglion-cell layer, and nerve-fiber layer approach the vitreous and optic nerve.

items.label: Cornea
items.detail: Transparent avascular layers run epithelium, Bowman's layer, regular stromal lamellae, Descemet membrane, endothelium.

items.label: Lens
items.detail: A thick capsule surrounds anterior subcapsular epithelium and elongated anucleate lens fibers.

items.label: Organ of Corti
items.detail: Hair cells and supporting cells sit on basilar membrane beneath the tectorial membrane within the cochlear duct.

items.label: Vestibular receptors
items.detail: Maculae have otolith-bearing membranes for linear acceleration; cristae project into cupulae for angular acceleration.

essentials: Light passes through inner retinal layers before reaching rods and cones near the pigment epithelium.
Photoreceptors synapse with bipolar cells, which synapse with ganglion cells; ganglion axons form the optic nerve.
Corneal transparency depends on regular collagen spacing, relative dehydration, avascularity, and smooth surfaces.
The organ of Corti transduces sound; vestibular hair cells transduce head position and acceleration.
Endolymph fills the membranous labyrinth, while perilymph surrounds it within the bony labyrinth.

traps.wrong: Photoreceptors form the retinal layer closest to vitreous because they receive light.
traps.right: They lie near the pigment epithelium on the outer side; light crosses the inner retina first.

traps.wrong: Bowman's and Descemet membranes are equivalent basal laminae on the same side of cornea.
traps.right: Bowman's is anterior beneath epithelium; Descemet is the posterior corneal endothelial basal lamina.

recognition: A dark pigment layer beside stacked nuclear and plexiform layers identifies retina.
A thick regular collagen stroma between two surface cell layers identifies cornea.
A triangular sensory complex on the basilar membrane identifies the organ of Corti.
